policy_title: Restore maintenance grants and scrap tuition fees for higher education
stated: Fully fund every higher education student by restoring maintenance grants and scrapping undergraduate tuition fees, with long-term plans to cancel graduate debt.

source.quote: We would fully fund every higher education student, restoring maintenance grants and scrapping undergraduate tuition fees. Our long-term plans also include seeking to cancel the injustice of graduate debt.

bearing_set.reason: Scrapping fees and restoring maintenance grants directly affects who can access higher education, especially for lower-income students, bearing materially on the attainment/access gap and opportunity.

Maintenance grants directly address students' ability to afford food, rent, and bills while studying; graduate debt cancellation would improve post-study disposable income — a real, non-negligible effect on cost of living for a substantial population.

Removing tuition fees eliminates the quasi-graduate-tax repayment (9% of income above threshold for up to 30 years) and debt cancellation directly improves take-home pay for current repaying graduates — a material move on the take-home-pay indicator.

Funding higher education publicly at scale requires multi-billion-pound annual commitments (IFS estimated free tuition alone at £5–8bn/yr); the funded-vs-borrowed indicator is materially affected, giving this a real public-finances verdict.

The distributional incidence is contested but non-negligible: fee abolition benefits the ~50% who attend university (average higher earners) while non-graduates gain nothing; maintenance grants are more progressive — the net effect on the rich-poor gap is a genuine, evidence-bearing question.

membership_note: Four fundamentals earn real verdicts: the designed-for outcome (O7, improves access), the household take-home-pay gain for graduates (O11), the fiscal cost to public borrowing (O12), and the distributional question of who actually benefits (O14 — direction contested by evidence).
